clue.text: Camel on the loose tucks into butter that sits on table

definitions.note: a relative clause with its noun left unsaid: read it as 'a thing that sits on table'

indicators.note: to tuck one thing into another is to push it inside, so the loosened letters go within the word for butter

parts.note: a pat is a small shaped lump of butter

indicators.note: an animal on the loose has broken free, so the letters of the word before it break out of their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A stray camel wanders up and helps itself to the butter dish on the dining table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butter' often means a ram or goat, something that butts, but here it is the dairy kind. 'on the loose' rearranges the camel into LACEM, which 'tucks into' the lump of butter.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a place mat is a small protective covering laid under each diner's plate, so it rests on the dining table.

clue.text: On ship notice pig that mates brought in

indicators.note: the notice has had the pig brought in, so the animal's name is carried inside the word for notice

parts.note: an ad, short for advertisement, is a public notice
a boar is an uncastrated male pig, the one kept for breeding

explanation.surface: A warning at sea: watch out for the pig that the ship's officers smuggled in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mates' reads as ship's officers, the subject of 'brought in', but it is a verb: the pig that mates is the breeding male. 'brought in' then puts that animal in the notice.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a passenger who is aboard is on a vessel, whether boat, train or aircraft.

clue.text: Flower personified in new arrangement for Hamlet's death

indicators.note: a new arrangement is a fresh ordering, so the letters of the three words after it are set out in a different order

parts.note: taken as written, fifteen letters once the apostrophe is dropped

explanation.surface: For Hamlet's death scene, a florist's new arrangement shows a blossom in human form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is the crossword trick for a river, a thing that flows; the Thames, London's river, is traditionally pictured as an old man. 'in new arrangement' rearranges the fifteen letters of 'for Hamlet's death'.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossword-only sense: a 'flower' is something that flows, a river, and this is the traditional name for London's river imagined as an old man.

clue.text: Particular responsibility Liberal finds acceptable in corrupt society

parts.note: your baby is a project or duty that is yours alone to look after: 'the budget is her baby'
L is the standard abbreviation for Liberal, as in election results
on means acceptable in British speech, heard mostly in the negative: 'that's just not on'

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician decides that one special duty is tolerable, even in a rotten society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finds' and 'in' only join the three pieces to the definition. ON for 'acceptable' is British usage, heard mostly in the negative: 'that's just not on'.
explanation.definitionFit: Byword: the ancient Mesopotamian city condemned in the Bible became a name for any decadent, oppressive social order.

clue.text: Fast Spanish fleet runs away — British ships to port and starboard?

indicators.note: port and starboard are a ship's left and right sides, so the navy's two letters go one at each side of what is left of the fleet

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy, Britain's fleet of warships

indicators.note: away sends the letter for runs out of the word for the Spanish fleet

parts.note: the Armada was the Spanish invasion fleet sent against England in 1588
R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A swift Spanish fleet flees, with British warships closing in on its left and right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like an adjective for the fleet; it is the noun, a month of fasting. 'away' takes R out of ARMADA, leaving AMADA, and 'to port and starboard' sets R and N on its left and right.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Ramadan is the Islamic holy month in which Muslims take no food or drink between dawn and sunset.

clue.text: Book good about free spirit connecting

indicators.note: about means around: the letters for book and good stand one on each side of the two words that follow

parts.note: B is a standard abbreviation for book, as in library catalogues
G is the abbreviation for good, as in grading scales such as VG, very good
to rid a place of something is to free it of that thing
gin is a distilled alcoholic spirit flavoured with juniper

explanation.surface: It is a good book about an unconventional soul who brings people together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'free spirit' is one phrase on the surface but two pieces, the verb 'free' and a spirit you can drink. 'about' has the single letters for book and good flank that pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a participle: bridging two things means spanning the gap so that they are linked, as a bridging loan does.

clue.text: A Labour leader of old being prepared

parts.note: Michael Foot led Britain's Labour Party, the main party of the left, from 1980 to 1983

explanation.surface: A veteran former head of the Labour Party is being made ready for something.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Foot led Britain's Labour Party from 1980 to 1983. 'being prepared' looks like something done to the leader, but it describes plans that are in hand: 'something is afoot'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: plans that are afoot are in preparation or already in progress.

clue.text: Surrealist birds, heading to the east

indicators.note: the heading is the first letter, and in an across answer east is the right-hand end, so that letter travels to the far end of the birds

parts.note: terns are slender seabirds related to gulls

explanation.surface: A flock of strange, dreamlike birds is flying off towards the east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading to the east' reads as a direction of flight; it sends the first letter of TERNS to the right-hand end, east on a map. Max Ernst was a German pioneer of Surrealism whose paintings are full of birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Max Ernst, the German-born painter and sculptor, was a founder of the Surrealist movement.

clue.text: Christian whose work caused feathers to fly?

definitions.meaning: the surname of the officer who led the 1789 mutiny on HMS Bounty; his first name is wanted

definitions.text: whose work caused feathers to fly
definitions.meaning: the old craftsman who fitted feathers to arrows, so that his handiwork flew from the bow

explanation.surface: A churchgoer whose efforts stirred up a furious quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: Fletcher Christian led the 1789 mutiny on HMS Bounty, so 'Christian' points to his forename. A fletcher made arrows, fitting their feathers, so 'feathers to fly' is literal, a playful twist on the idiom for a furious row.
explanation.definitionFit: Forename and trade: Fletcher Christian led the Bounty mutineers, and a fletcher is an arrow-maker whose feathered shafts flew from the bow.

clue.text: One soft cheese and one firm in crumbly tart

indicators.note: in says the letters for one and firm sit inside the crumbled word that follows
something crumbly breaks into bits, so the letters of the next word fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one; this is the clue's second 'one', the first belonging to the definition
a firm is a company, abbreviated Co

explanation.surface: One soft cheese and one hard one are baked together in a flaky pastry case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firm' pretends to be the opposite of soft, a second cheese; it is a company. 'crumbly' rearranges the tart into RTTA, and 'in' drops the numeral and the company into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: ricotta is a mild white Italian whey cheese with a moist, spoonable texture.

clue.text: Wrong skill shown by a backing singer

parts.note: a wrong is a sin, an offence against what is right

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the skill and the a after it are read from right to left as one run

parts.note: art is skill, as in 'the art of conversation'

explanation.surface: A supporting vocalist is displaying a faulty technique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing singer' reads as one phrase, a supporting vocalist, but splits: 'backing' turns ART and A together into ATRA, leaving 'singer' alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Frank Sinatra was the American vocalist famous for 'My Way' and 'New York, New York'.

clue.text: Catharine Glover an Australian blonde!

definitions.meaning: the heroine of an 1828 novel by Sir Walter Scott, a glover's daughter known by the nickname in its title
a playful description of a light-haired young woman from the capital of Western Australia

explanation.surface: Catharine Glover turns out, to general surprise, to be a blonde from Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: Catharine Glover is the heroine of Walter Scott's novel The Fair Maid of Perth, set in Scotland. The exclamation mark flags the cheeky second reading: Perth is also a city in Western Australia, and a fair maid a blonde girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Title and joke: Catharine Glover is the heroine of Scott's novel of this name, and a light-haired girl from Western Australia's capital would earn the same description.

clue.text: Channel swimmer crosses river

indicators.note: to cross a river is to span it from bank to bank, so the swimmer's letters stand on both sides of the river's

parts.note: a tench is a freshwater fish of the carp family; crosswords call any fish a swimmer
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Someone swimming the English Channel also makes it across a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Channel swimmer' looks like one phrase, someone swimming the sea between England and France; split it. 'Channel' alone is the definition, the swimmer is a fish, and 'crosses' wraps TENCH round R.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a trench is a long narrow ditch dug in the ground, such as one cut for drainage.

clue.text: Swing he composed to include hint of Ravel?

definitions.text: Swing he composed to include hint of Ravel?

indicators.note: to include says the reworked letters take the extra letter in among them
to compose is to put together, so the letters of the two words before it are put together afresh

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a hint of something is its smallest trace, here just the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A composer wrote swing music with just a trace of Ravel's style in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' rearranges SWING HE into GESHWIN and 'to include' slots in R, the 'hint of' Ravel. The whole clue is also the definition: George Gershwin wrote jazz-age music and admired Ravel, once asking him for lessons.
explanation.definitionFit: Whole-clue description: George Gershwin was the American composer of jazz-age songs and concert works who admired Ravel and asked him for lessons.

clue.text: Public house open — beer regularly supplies American flyer

parts.note: PH marks a public house, the full name for a pub, on British maps

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals: take every other letter of the two words before it, starting with the first

explanation.surface: The pub is open, and its beer keeps an American airman regularly supplied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the odd-numbered letters of OPEN BEER, the dash being only punctuation. The 'flyer' is a bird, not an airman: the phoebe is a North American flycatcher.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a phoebe is a small North American bird of the tyrant-flycatcher family, named for its two-note call.

clue.text: Perhaps Ayckbourn inspires black star

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so the playwright's first name draws the next word inside itself

parts.note: Sir Alan Ayckbourn is a prolific English playwright; perhaps shows he is just one bearer of the first name
to black goods or a workplace is British trade-union usage for boycotting them, which is to debar them

explanation.surface: A playwright such as Ayckbourn is the creative spark behind a black leading actor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inspires' reads as 'motivates' but means 'breathes in', so the playwright's first name takes the next piece into itself. 'black' is a verb, British trade-union usage for boycotting goods or a workplace.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Aldebaran is the bright orange-red giant that marks the eye of the bull in the constellation Taurus.

clue.text: Contacted Irishman seen upside-down in rising river

indicators.note: in says the Irishman's name, once turned over, sits inside the river's
in a down answer, rising means read from the bottom up, so the river's name is written backwards

parts.note: the Dee is a river that flows through north Wales and the English city of Chester

indicators.note: in a down answer, a word seen upside-down reads from bottom to top, so the Irishman's name is written backwards

parts.note: Liam is a common Irish man's name, the Irish short form of William

explanation.surface: Rescuers got in touch with an Irishman spotted capsized in a swelling river.
explanation.walkthrough: Both names are turned over, each by its own indicator: 'seen upside-down' makes the Irishman MAIL, 'rising' makes the river EED, and 'in' puts the first into the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym in the past tense: someone you emailed is someone you got in touch with by electronic message.

clue.text: Like female with shocked appearance?

parts.note: as and like both introduce a comparison: 'white as a sheet', 'white like a sheet'
a hen is a female bird, and informally a woman, as in hen party

explanation.surface: Similar to a woman who looks as if she has had a nasty fright.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one description of a startled woman, but only the last three words define. Shock is just one reason a face goes grey-white like ash, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: an ashen face is drained of colour, grey-white like ash, the look of someone who has had a bad fright.

clue.text: Historical land half devoured by snake?

indicators.note: whatever a snake devours ends up inside it, so the word for half goes within the snake's name

parts.note: a boa is a large snake that crushes its prey
hemi- is the Greek prefix meaning half, as in hemisphere

explanation.surface: An ancient country, half of it swallowed up by a serpent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' tempts you to cut a word in two; it is a Greek prefix, taken whole, and 'devoured by' puts it in the snake. Bohemia was a central European kingdom, now the western Czech Republic.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Bohemia was a medieval kingdom of central Europe, now the western part of the Czech Republic.

clue.text: Akhtar mediates to provide with weapon

indicators.note: a loose signal: the two words before it provide the solution because its letters run unbroken across the gap between them

explanation.surface: Akhtar steps in as go-between, with the aim of supplying a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to provide' is a loose signal that the two words before it hold the answer across their join. The definition is only 'with weapon'; 'to provide with weapon' would define ARM, not ARMED.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjectival phrase: an armed guard is a guard carrying a gun or other means of attack.

clue.text: In part decline to accept appeal by newspaper

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so the word for decline opens up and holds the other two pieces

parts.note: to die away is to decline or fade: 'the wind died'

indicators.note: by means beside, without saying which side: here the appeal comes straight after the newspaper

parts.note: The Sun is a British tabloid daily
it is an old word for sex appeal, as in 'she has it' or 'It girl'

explanation.surface: Partly refuse to take up a plea launched by a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In part' reads as 'partly', but only 'part', the verb meaning separate, defines; 'In' merely leads into the clue. 'to accept' has the word for decline take in the other two, which 'by' sets next to each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a verb: to disunite people is to separate them or set them at odds, just as to part them is.

clue.text: Suspend start of play when second side changes

indicators.note: left and right are the two sides, and the word for a play's opening holds the abbreviation of each; the later one switches to the opposite side

parts.note: a prologue is the introductory speech that opens a play

explanation.surface: Hold up the beginning of the match until the second team has changed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a delayed match. PROLOGUE holds both sides, R for right then L for left; 'when second side changes' flips the later one, L, to R.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to prorogue a parliament is to discontinue its sittings for a time without dissolving it.

clue.text: In French one barbed comment is demeaning

parts.note: Fr is the standard abbreviation for French, as in dictionary etymologies
a is the indefinite article, another way of saying one: 'a dozen', 'one dozen'
a dig is a pointed, sarcastic remark aimed at someone

explanation.surface: Said in French, a single cutting remark is degrading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In French one' wants to be UN or UNE, but each word is its own piece and 'is' only joins. Infra dig is short for the Latin infra dignitatem, 'beneath one's dignity'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: infra dig, from the Latin for 'beneath dignity', describes something degrading or unworthy of one's position.

clue.text: Extra sweetheart topless and shy

indicators.note: in a down answer the top is the first letter, so the word for sweetheart loses its opening letter

parts.note: a lover is a sweetheart, the person one is in love with
to shy is to throw, as at a coconut shy, the British fairground stall where balls are thrown at coconuts

explanation.surface: A spare girlfriend, bare-chested yet bashful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' takes the L off LOVER, leaving OVER. 'shy' is not bashful but the verb throw, as at a fairground coconut shy; in cricket an overthrow is an extra run from a fielder's wild return.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket sense: an overthrow is a bonus run taken when a fielder's return goes astray, though strictly not one of the scorer's 'extras'.

clue.text: Equip with new parts — bent lever ultimately lifts it

indicators.note: in a down answer, something that lifts rises from the bottom, so the two pieces before it are read upwards as one run

parts.note: a bent is a natural talent or inclination, which is what your forte is

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end: take the final letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: To fit new components: a crooked lever eventually raises the machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bent' looks like an adjective for the lever; it is the noun for a natural aptitude. 'ultimately' adds the lever's last letter to it, and 'lifts' reads the resulting FORTER upwards as RETROF.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to retrofit a machine or building is to fit it with components it did not have when first made.

clue.text: Esoteric octet holds note with ritualistic symbolism

indicators.note: holds says the reworked word before it has the note inside it
an unusual, loose signal: esoteric means obscure, hard to make out, so the letters of the next word are obscured by a change of order

parts.note: taken as written
mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale: do, re, mi

explanation.surface: A mysterious eight-piece ensemble sustains a note full of ritual meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Esoteric' is an unusual anagram signal, obscure in the sense of hard to make out: it rearranges the octet into TOTEC, which 'holds' the sol-fa note.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjectival phrase: something totemic stands as a revered emblem, like the carved pole that represents a clan.

clue.text: Party food in tin with mushy peas

parts.note: a tin is the British word for a can of food

indicators.note: something mushy has been mashed out of shape, so the letters of the next word are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Buffet nibbles served from a can alongside mashed peas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mushy' rearranges PEAS into APES; 'in' and 'with' only join. Mushy peas, a soft green mash, are the classic side dish at a British fish-and-chip shop, far from dainty party food.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: canapés are bite-sized savouries on bread or pastry, handed round with drinks at receptions.

clue.text: Prophet beat up on Chinese people

indicators.note: in a down answer, on means on top of: the upturned word sits above the Chinese people
in a down answer, up means read from the bottom to the top, so the word for beat is written backwards

parts.note: to tan someone is to thrash or beat them, as in 'tan his hide'
the Han are the majority ethnic group of China

explanation.surface: A prophet gave some Chinese people a beating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beat up on' reads as one phrasal verb, to attack, but each word has its own job: 'up' turns the word for beat into NAT, and 'on' stacks it above the Chinese people. Nathan is the Old Testament prophet who rebuked King David.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Nathan is the Old Testament seer at King David's court who rebuked him over Bathsheba.

clue.text: Agree that man must enter church

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so the word for that man goes within the church's two letters

parts.note: CE is the Church of England, England's established church
him is the pronoun for a man already pointed out, 'that man'

explanation.surface: Everyone concurs that the fellow has to go into the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that' looks like a conjunction after 'Agree' but belongs with 'man', giving a pronoun, which 'must enter' the Church of England's initials. To chime with something is to be in accord with it.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to chime with something is to harmonise or be consistent with it, as bells rung together are in accord.

clue.text: Time to wear exclusive garment

indicators.note: what you wear goes around you, so the letter for time is clothed in the word for exclusive

parts.note: sole means exclusive, belonging to one only: 'sole rights'
T is the standard abbreviation for time, as in physics formulae

explanation.surface: It is the moment to put on a designer outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to wear' works from the wearer's side: clothes go round the body, so T is clothed in SOLE and ends up inside it. 'exclusive' is not chic here but 'belonging to one alone', as in sole rights.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a stole is a long scarf or shawl draped over the shoulders, by women as a wrap or by clergy as a vestment.
